Philippists
fi-lip'ists
n. pl. (the Philippists, the party of Melanchthon's followers in the German churches, c. 1550–1580)
From Philipp Melanchthon, Greek Philippos, lover of horses; with the suffix -ist, a follower or adherent.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Philippists were the men who held Wittenberg after Luther died and took their name from Philipp Melanchthon, whose learning, caution and horror of conflict they inherited together. They were not a sect and never meant to be a party; they were the university establishment, and the label was fastened on them by opponents. Three things divided them from the Gnesio-Lutherans: they defended the Leipzig Interim's concession of ceremonies, they spoke of the will as somehow cooperating in conversion, and on the Lord's Supper they moved steadily toward a position their enemies called Crypto-Calvinism — Christ truly received by faith rather than bodily present in the elements. In 1574 the elector of Saxony, convinced he had been deceived about how far the Wittenberg men had gone, arrested their leaders and broke the party; the Formula of Concord in 1577 wrote the Gnesio-Lutheran settlement into the confession. The irony is not small: on the Supper the Philippists were nearer the truth than the men who defeated them, and they lost anyway, because a party that will not say plainly what it believes cannot be defended when the test comes. “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines crypto as a prefix denoting concealment, and party as a number of persons united in opinion, in opposition to others.

PAR'TY, n. A number of persons united in opinion or design, in opposition to others in the community.

CRYP'TICAL, a. Hidden; secret; occult.

DISSIM'ULATION, n. The act of dissembling; a hiding under a false appearance.

SCHISM, n. In a general sense, division or separation; a division or separation in a church.

Key Scripture

1Co 1:10 — "Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment."

2Ti 1:13 — "Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus."

Rom 16:17 — "Now I beseech you, brethren, mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them."

Isa 8:20 — "To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them."

Modern Corruption

Melanchthon's heirs, broken in 1574 for holding quietly what they would not confess plainly.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the strategy the Philippists adopted and which is still recommended as prudence: hold the better view, teach it by implication, avoid the word that would force a decision, and wait for the climate to change. It does not work, and the reason is not tactical. A conviction that is never stated is never defended, and when the elector finally asked the Wittenberg men directly what they believed about the Supper, the years of careful ambiguity counted against them rather than for them.

The principle to recover is that the apostolic call to unity is a call to say the same thing out loud, not to leave the disputed thing unsaid. “that ye all speak the same thing” (1Co 1:10) is a demand for a common confession, and the measure of it is public: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20). Paul's charge to Timothy is about a form of sound words precisely because a form can be held out where a private persuasion cannot.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek schisma (G4978), a rent, a division; hupotuposis (G5296), a pattern, an outline form.

Greek schisma (G4978) — a rent, a cleft, a division; 1 Corinthians 1:10.

Greek katartizo (G2675) — to mend, to perfectly join together; 1 Corinthians 1:10.

Greek hupotuposis (G5296) — an outline, a pattern, a form; 2 Timothy 1:13.

Greek dichostasia (G1370) — a standing apart, a dissension; Romans 16:17.

Hebrew teudah (H8584) — testimony, attestation; Isaiah 8:20.

Usage

"“that ye all speak the same thing” (1Co 1:10) — what a party of careful silences could not do."

"“Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13) — Wittenberg, before the arrests of 1574."

"“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the measure no ambiguity survives."
